newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan shilling recoups losses after intervention.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan shilling recoups losses after intervention.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling recouped heavy losses on account of violent political unrest this week after the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) offloaded $29 million into the market, Governor Micah Cheserem told Reuters on Friday.

One commercial bank that bid 61.50 to the dollar early on Friday adjusted that to 58.60 at close. Cheserem said the central bank was standing by to meet any demand next Monday but indications were that pressure on the market was easing.
It was the largest amount of dollars the central bank has sold to calm a jittery market for several years, dealers said.
Dealers said that market reaction was swift. There was little demand for dollars after the central bank's show of strength, mainly during the morning trading session on Friday.
Most commercial banks fell back to rates of around 57 to 59 shillings against the dollar after opening at in the 59-61 range and maintaining spreads as wide as three shillings.
Signals from the central bank that it had more dollars than market demand was expected to calm market nerves and see shilling gains, senior dealers said.
"We have sold around $29 million today and everyone is satisfied. The more important thing is the perceptions (investors have) on the political front," Cheserem said.
"There may be more demand on Monday, we are standing by to meet any," Cheserem added.

Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the worst clashes between police and protesters since a violent campaign in July 1990 that helped persuade President Daniel arap Moi to allow multi-party politics. The protests have upset investors and made many wary of this emerging market.

Moi, speaking at a rally in western Kenya on Friday, blamed the opposition for the violence and added that negative effects such as a weakening shilling and rising cost of services and goods would hit ordinary people.
"The rate had gotten out of hand and central bank has to stabilise the shilling. If the rate is to move, it has to move in a gradual manner," one central bank official said.
The unrest also affected the Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE) where turnover was posted at 93.2 million shillings for the week ending Friday compared to 170.9 million shillings last week.
A total of 1.3 million shares were traded this week compared to 38.8 million shares traded in the previous week.
"There has been overeaction in the market," Cheserem said earlier, adding quoted rates for the shilling were ridiculous.
The shilling last touched the 60 range and threatened further losses versus the dollar in October 1993.
Cheserem, 47, who is one of Kenya's leading economic reform leaders, said one bank asked for $5 million but took only $1 million when the bank said it would meet the demand.
Another official at the central bank said state utility Kenya Power & Lighting Corp asked for $6.5 million but then backed down after the bank also said it would meet the demand.
Cheserem said the market would calm as both sides of Kenya's political divide settled their differences. "The biggest word in town is dialogue. Dialogue in block letters."
